l: poetry, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, INTRODUCTION.
s: Poetry was Ovid’s natural inclination and lasting vocation, although his father initially discouraged him from pursuing it. Ovid eventually abandoned law and public life for poetry, gained distinguished friends and admirers, and wrote works including the Metamorphoses.

l: Augustus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, INTRODUCTION.
s: Augustus was displeased by one of Ovid’s compositions because of its immoral tendency. He ordered Ovid to leave Rome and live at Tomi, possibly in connection with scandals involving Julia and his granddaughter.

l: Tomi, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, INTRODUCTION.
s: Tomi was a colony on the shore of the Euxine sea to which Augustus ordered Ovid to withdraw. Ovid lived there in banishment until his death in 18 A.D.

l: Ovid's exile, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, INTRODUCTION.
s: Ovid’s exile began when Augustus ordered him to leave Rome for Tomi around 8 A.D. Its exact cause remained unclear, though it was probably connected to an objectionable composition and scandals involving members of Augustus’s family. Ovid never returned to Rome and died in banishment at Tomi.

s: The Metamorphoses presents a design to speak of forms changed into new bodies. The speaker asks the Gods to favor the attempt because they changed the forms. The narrative is to extend from the beginning of the world to the speaker’s own times.

s: The Metamorphoses presents a design to speak of forms changed into new bodies.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The notes discuss the phrase “Forms changed into new bodies” and whether it is an instance of Hypallage. They explain that “formæ” can sometimes mean the things themselves, including gods or wild beasts, so the phrase may not involve deliberate word transposition. They also explain “adspirate” as a metaphor from winds filling sails and remark that the invocation is perhaps too brief for a work as grave as the Metamorphoses. “My own times” refers to the days of Augustus Cæsar.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: The Metamorphoses is described as a grave and dignified work whose opening invocation may be insufficiently long or elaborate. Its subject concerns the changes and variations of bodies, introduced through the phrase “Forms changed into new bodies.”

l: Augustus Cæsar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes
s: “My own times” is explained as referring to the days of Augustus Cæsar.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: God and bounteous Nature bring order to Chaos, the rude and undigested mass that initially fills the universe. God separates the earth, waters, heavens, and atmosphere, then places the elements in harmonious arrangement. The fiery heaven rises highest, the air lies beneath it, the Earth settles below them, and the waters surround the solid globe.

l: God, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: God, with bounteous Nature, ends the discord in Chaos by separating the earth from the heavens, the waters from the earth, and the clear heavens from the gross atmosphere. He combines the separated elements in harmonious unison and assigns each to its proper place.

l: Chaos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Chaos is the name men give to the original state of the universe, in which the sea, the earth, and the heaven form a rude, undigested mass. Its discord is ended when God and bounteous Nature separate and arrange its elements.

l: Nature, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Bounteous Nature joins God in putting an end to the discord of Chaos. Together with God, she helps separate and harmoniously arrange the elements.

l: universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: At first, the universe contains only the sea, the earth, and the heaven, all mixed together in Chaos. It is subsequently ordered as the separated elements take their proper places.

l: Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The sea is initially mixed with the earth, heaven, and air, making it unnavigable. After the elements are separated, the waters sink to the lowest place and surround the solid globe.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Earth is initially without firmness because it is mixed with the sea and air. It is separated from the heavens and waters, then settles below the lighter elements, drawing ponderous atoms and being pressed together by its own gravity.

l: Heaven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The heaven initially covers all things and is mixed with the earth, sea, and air. After being distinguished from the gross atmosphere, its fiery and weightless element occupies the highest region.

l: Air, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The air is initially mixed with the land and sea and is void of light. Once separated from the other elements, it takes the place next to the heaven in both lightness and position.

l: four elements, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The elements are initially confused and discordant, with cold opposed to hot, moist to dry, soft to hard, and heavy things to weightless things. God and bounteous Nature separate them and place them in harmonious order.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the ancient belief that Chaos was pre-existent matter given form and order by a powerful cause. It contrasts this belief with the account of creation in the Book of Genesis, suggesting that mythological traditions preserve a confused version of that account. Hesiod is identified as the first poet to discuss Chaos extensively, while Sanchoniatho is said to have influenced Greek ideas about it. The notes also explain mythological terms associated with the formation and ordering of the universe.

l: Chaos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Chaos is described as pre-existent matter without form or order, from which the ordered world was formed. The ancient philosophers believed that a powerful cause arranged its elements according to their qualities.

l: God, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: God is presented in the explanation as the powerful cause whose invisible agency reduces Chaos to order. The ancient system described in the unit does not treat God as the Creator, but as the one who organizes pre-existent matter.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Earth is described as having existed in a differently arranged form before receiving order. In the account of the elements, it occupies the central or solid region, while the waters surround or occupy lower channels relative to its surface.

l: universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The universe is described through ancient theories as having been formed by arranging pre-existent matter and its elements. Sanchoniatho is said to have transmitted ideas about its original construction through a priest of Jehovah.

l: world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The world’s formation is treated as a confused mythological tradition concerning the ordering of Chaos. The unit says that this tradition contains a faint reflection of the creation account in the Book of Genesis.

l: God as architect of the universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: God as architect of the universe is described as arranging and disposing pre-existent elements in places suited to their qualities. In this ancient philosophical system, God is regarded as the Architect rather than the Creator.

l: the creation of the world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The creation of the world is explained through both mythological accounts of Chaos and the account in the Book of Genesis. The unit argues that the mythological system is a confused and disfigured tradition of the creation described by Moses.

l: Hesiod, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Hesiod is identified as the most ancient heathen writer to enlarge upon the subject of the world’s formation. He is also said to have been the first to mention Chaos and to have derived much of his information from Sanchoniatho.

l: Genesis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Book of Genesis is presented as a source that sheds light on the mythological account of the world’s formation. Its first two chapters describe the creation of the world, including darkness spread over the deep.

l: Sanchoniatho, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Sanchoniatho is said to have lived before the Trojan war and to have written in the Phœnician language. He claimed to have received information about the original construction of the world from a priest of Jehovah named Jerombaal, and the Greeks may have borrowed their ideas about Chaos from him.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: God divides the separated mass into distinct parts and gives the universe its forms, boundaries, climates, waters, winds, stars, and living creatures. The Earth receives plains, valleys, woods, mountains, waters, wild beasts, and eventually Man. Prometheus fashions Man from earth tempered with water, after the image of the Gods, and Man is animated by Minerva. Man is distinguished from other animals by his upright form and ability to look toward the heavens.

l: God, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: God, or the Artificer of all things, divides the mass into distinct members, shapes it into a globe, and orders the sea, rivers, landforms, climates, air, winds, stars, and living creatures. He gives Man a countenance that looks upward toward the heavens.

l: Prometheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Prometheus, the son of Iapetus, fashions Man from earth tempered with water, shaping him after the image of the Gods.

l: universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The universe is formed from a separated mass that is divided into distinct members and ordered into land, waters, air, heavens, climates, stars, and living creatures.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Earth is shaped into a globe and marked with plains, valleys, woods, mountains, rivers, lakes, and different climates. It receives wild beasts and provides the material from which Prometheus fashions Man.

l: mankind, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Man is formed from earth tempered with water and is made after the image of the Gods. Unlike other animals, he stands upright and looks toward the heavens and the stars; Minerva animates him.

l: the creation of the world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The formation of the world proceeds through the separation and ordering of matter, followed by the creation of landforms, waters, climates, winds, stars, and living creatures. Man is formed last as a being capable of ruling over the rest.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains that Ovid’s account of creation resembles Genesis, especially in presenting man as the Creator’s final work. It identifies the Creator with God, who formed man from divine elements and gave him dominion over other living things. It further interprets Prometheus as tempering the earth and Minerva as animating his workmanship, together reflecting God’s formation and animation of man. The notes also describe the ordering of the earth, heavens, waters, zones, and winds.

l: God, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: God is presented as the Creator who formed man from divine elements and gave him dominion over the other living works of creation. The unit compares Ovid’s account of God breathing life into man with the account in Genesis.

l: Genesis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Genesis is cited as describing God’s creation of light and the granting of dominion to man over the fish, birds, and living things of the earth. The unit says that Ovid’s account presents information derived from Holy Writ in a disfigured form.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The earth is divided into torrid, temperate, and frigid zones corresponding to divisions in the heavens. Prometheus is said to temper the earth when making man.

l: mankind, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Man is described as the last work of the Creator, formed from divine elements so that he could rule over the other animated works of creation. His animation is compared with God breathing the breath of life into him.

l: Prometheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Prometheus is described as tempering the earth in the making of man. Some writers identify him with a Scriptural character, while the unit also notes traditions that associate him with teaching mankind to produce fire and with the invention or improvement of metalworking.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Minerva is described as animating the workmanship of Prometheus. Together with Prometheus, she represents aspects of God’s formation and animation of man.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The formation of man is followed by the succession of the four ages of the world, beginning with the Golden Age. During the Golden Age, Innocence and Justice govern the world without laws, punishment, or fear. Men live safely and peacefully, without war, soldiers, or concern for foreign shores. The Earth produces food freely, and an eternal spring brings abundant crops, milk, nectar, and honey.

l: four ages of the world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The four ages of the world follow the formation of man. The Golden Age is the first of them.

l: Golden Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Golden Age is founded first and is governed by Innocence and Justice. During it, men live without laws, punishment, war, or fear, while the Earth produces food abundantly.

l: world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The world is governed by Innocence and Justice during the Golden Age. It has no avenger, threatening decrees, or need for soldiers.

l: Innocence, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Innocence governs the world during the Golden Age.

l: Justice, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Justice governs the world during the Golden Age.

l: laws, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Laws do not govern the Golden Age. Men practise faith and rectitude without them.

l: mortals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Men live safely and peacefully during the Golden Age, without fear, soldiers, or warlike weapons. They gather fruits, berries, cornels, and acorns, and eat food produced freely by the Earth.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Earth is untouched by the harrow and uninjured by ploughshares. It produces food of its own accord, yields crops without ploughing, and provides rivers of milk and nectar as well as honey from the green holm oak.

l: perpetual spring, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: An eternal spring exists during the Golden Age. Gentle Zephyrs foster flowers that grow without seed.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The explanation says that the heathen poets probably learned from tradition that the first parents initially lived in peaceful innocence. The garden of Eden supplied them with abundant fruit and food without tillage, and animals obeyed them. After the fall, the ground became unfruitful without labor, and nature no longer spontaneously acknowledged man as master. The poets called the happier earlier period the Golden Age, while Latin writers placed corresponding events in Italy under Saturn and Janus; the Scriptures relate them in the histories of Adam and Noah.

l: heathen poets, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The heathen poets probably learned from tradition about the peaceful innocence of the first parents, the abundance of the garden of Eden, and the later effects of the fall. They called the happier period the Golden Age and placed it in their own countries.

l: first parents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The first parents initially lived in peaceful innocence. They had abundant food without tillage, and the animals were submissive to their commands.

l: garden of Eden, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The garden of Eden furnished the first parents with fruit and food in abundance without tillage.

l: fall, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: After the fall, the ground became unfruitful and yielded nothing without labor. Nature no longer spontaneously acknowledged man as its master.

l: Golden Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Golden Age was the name the poets gave to the more happy days of the first parents, a time associated with innocence.

l: Latin writers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Latin writers placed in Italy, under the reign of Saturn and Janus, events that the Scriptures relate in the histories of Adam and Noah.

l: Italy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Italy was identified by the Latin writers as the setting for the events associated with the Golden Age.

l: Saturn, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Saturn was described as reigning over the events that Latin writers placed in Italy and associated with the Golden Age.

l: Janus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Janus was described as reigning with Saturn over the events that Latin writers placed in Italy and associated with the Golden Age.

l: Scriptures, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Scriptures relate the corresponding events in the histories of Adam and Noah.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: After Saturn is driven into Tartarus, Jupiter rules the world and the Silver Age follows the Golden Age. In the Silver Age, Jupiter divides the year into four seasons, and men begin building shelters and cultivating the earth. The Brazen Age is fiercer and more warlike, while the Iron Age brings crime, fraud, violence, greed, warfare, and the breakdown of family and social bonds. Astræa, the virgin goddess, is the last of the heavenly deities to leave the Earth, which is drenched in slaughter.

l: Silver Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Silver Age succeeds the Golden Age under Jupiter's rule. It is less happy and less just than the Golden Age but more valuable than the Brazen Age; during it, the year is divided into four seasons, men build primitive houses, and they begin burying seeds and using oxen to plow.

l: Golden Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Golden Age is presented as a time when men are more just and consequently happier than in the Silver Age.

l: Brazen Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Brazen Age succeeds the Silver Age as the third age. Its people are fiercer and more inclined to horrible warfare, though they are still free from impiety.

l: Iron Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Iron Age is the last age and is marked by degenerated tendencies. Crime, fraud, deceit, treachery, violence, greed, warfare, murder, and the collapse of family loyalty appear in it.

l: Saturn, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Saturn is driven into the shady realms of Tartarus before Jupiter rules the world.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter rules the world after Saturn is driven into Tartarus. He shortens the former perpetual spring and divides the year into winter, summer, autumn, and spring.

l: world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The world comes under Jupiter's sway after Saturn's expulsion. Under the changing ages, it passes from the more virtuous conditions of the Golden Age into the violence and corruption of the Iron Age.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Earth is first used for cultivation when the seeds of Ceres are buried in furrows. Its land, once common, is later divided by boundaries, and its entrails are mined for riches; by the end, it is drenched in slaughter.

l: humanity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Humanity becomes progressively less virtuous after the Golden Age. Men begin making shelters, farming, sailing, measuring and claiming land, mining for riches, and committing violence, betrayal, murder, and other crimes.

l: War, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: War appears in the Iron Age after destructive iron and gold emerge. It fights through the means of both and brandishes clattering weapons in its blood-stained hands.

l: crime, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Crime bursts forth in the Iron Age in every form. It includes fraud, deceit, treachery, violence, greed, rapine, murder, and the poisoning of family members.

l: wickedness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Vice is encouraged by the riches dug from the Earth, which had hidden them and removed them to the Stygian shades. Its rise accompanies the degeneration of the Iron Age.

l: Astræa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Astræa is a virgin and the last of the heavenly deities to abandon the Earth. She leaves only after the Earth has become drenched in slaughter.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The explanation describes the successive Golden, Silver, Brazen, and Iron Ages as stages in humanity’s decline from innocence to wickedness. During the Golden Age, perpetual spring prevailed, while the Silver Age introduced the division of the year into seasons, and the Iron Age continues into the present. It also notes inconsistencies in ancient accounts, including wars and crimes during Saturn’s Golden Age. Saturn expelled his father and seized his throne, Jupiter later treated Saturn similarly, and Jupiter fought the Giants when they tried to dispossess him of the heavens.

l: Astræa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Astræa was the Goddess of Justice. After leaving the earth, she was believed to have taken her place among the stars as the Constellation of the Virgin.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter treated Saturn as Saturn had treated his father Uranus. Jupiter also waged war against the Giants when they attempted to dispossess him of the heavens.

l: Golden Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: During the Golden Age, perpetual spring reigned on the earth, and the division of the year into seasons was not known. The account is presented as inconsistent because wars and crimes are also said to have occurred during Saturn’s Golden Age.

l: Silver Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Silver Age succeeded the Golden Age. During it, the year was divided into seasons.

l: Iron Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Iron Age followed the Brazen Age and still continues. It represents the later stage of humanity’s degeneration into wickedness and impiety.

l: Saturn, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Saturn expelled his father and seized his throne. His Golden Age is associated with perpetual spring, although ancient accounts also place wars and crimes within it.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Giants attempt to become masters of heaven by piling mountains up to the stars. Jupiter defeats them with lightning, burying their bodies beneath the mountains they assembled. Earth is drenched with their blood and forms a fierce generation of men from it, but this new generation also despises the Gods above and delights in violence.

l: Giants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Giants aspire to rule heaven and pile mountains together to reach the stars. Jupiter strikes them down with lightning and buries them beneath their own structure.

l: Heaven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Giants attempt to gain sovereignty over heaven, making its lofty realms seem unsafe.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Earth is drenched with the abundant blood of the Giants’ sons. She gives life to the warm blood and shapes it into men so that the ruthless race will not lack a memorial.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter, called the omnipotent Father, hurls lightning at the Giants, breaks through their mountain structure, and strikes Ossa away from Pelion.

l: mountains, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Giants heap mountains together in an assault on heaven, piling them up to the lofty stars. The mountains then overwhelm and bury the Giants.

l: blood, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The blood of the Giants’ sons drenches Earth and gives life to a new generation. Its origin in blood is reflected in that generation’s violence and greed for slaughter.

l: generation sprung from the blood of the Giants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Earth forms the generation of men from the warm blood of the Giants’ sons. This generation despises the Gods above, is greedy for ruthless slaughter, and is full of violence.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The notes explain that the Giants are said to have piled Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa on one another to reach heaven. The explanation distinguishes the war of the giants from the war between Jupiter and the Titans, who were inhabitants of heaven. It suggests that the fall of the angels may have inspired the story of the Titans, while the building of the tower of Babel may have inspired the Giants’ attempt to reach heaven. It also proposes that the descendants of Cain may correspond to the people described in Scripture as the children “of men” and “giants.”

l: Heaven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Giants attempted to reach heaven by piling Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa one upon another.

l: Giants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Giants are said to have heaped Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa together in an attempt to scale heaven. Their story may have been influenced by the building of the tower of Babel.

l: the war of the Gods with the Giants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The war of the giants is distinguished from the war between Jupiter and the Titans. It concerns the Giants’ attempt to reach heaven.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter is associated with the war against the Titans, which is presented as distinct from the war of the giants.

l: Titans, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Titans are described as inhabitants of heaven. Their story may have arisen from traditions about the fall of the angels.

l: fall of the angels, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The fall of the angels is suggested as a possible source for the story of the Titans.

l: angels, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The angels are said to have fallen, according to tradition, and this fall may have contributed to the story of the Titans.

l: tower of Babel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The building of the tower of Babel may have laid the foundation for the story of the Giants’ attempt to reach heaven.

l: attempt by the giants to reach heaven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The attempt by the Giants to reach heaven is represented by their piling mountains one upon another. It may have been based on the building of the tower of Babel.

l: descendants of Cain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The descendants of Cain may have been the people described in Scripture as the children “of men” and “giants.” They may also have been represented under the form of the Giants and as the generation sprung from their blood.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter sees the crimes of the human race and summons the Gods to decide the destruction of the world. He recalls Lycaon's polluted banquet and says that Lycaon has plotted against him, leading the Gods to demand vengeance. Jupiter declares that mortals must be cut off because their corruption cannot be cured, and he explains that he descended to Earth in human form to investigate the reports of wrongdoing. The Gods' unanimous alarm is compared with the Romans' reaction when an impious band sought to destroy the Roman name in the blood of Cæsar, and with the subjects' devotion to Augustus.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter beholds the crimes of the human race, recalls Lycaon's polluted banquet, and summons a council of the Gods. He declares that the race of mortals must be destroyed because their corruption cannot be cured, and says that he descended from Olympus in human form to examine the earth and found the reality worse than reported.

l: the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gods assemble in Jupiter's marble hall and listen to his accusations against the human race and Lycaon. They shout their assent and call for vengeance, then fall silent when Jupiter suppresses their clamor.

l: grand council of the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The council of the Gods is summoned by Jupiter to determine how to respond to the crimes of the impious race of men. It meets without delay in the heavenly assembly hall.

l: Lycaon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Lycaon is associated with a polluted banquet and is described as remarkable for his cruelty. He has formed a plot against Jupiter, and Jupiter states that he has suffered dire punishment.

l: mankind, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The race of mortals is condemned by Jupiter because guilt and corruption are found throughout the earth. Jupiter declares that it must be cut off so that the sound parts will not be corrupted.

l: Deucalion's deluge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The destruction of the world is the purpose for which Jupiter calls the council of the Gods. Jupiter determines that the mortal race must be destroyed, though the unit does not describe the destruction itself taking place.

l: universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The world is threatened with destruction because of the crimes of the impious human race. Jupiter says that he surveyed the earth and found that the reports of its iniquity were less serious than the reality.

l: Augustus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Augustus is addressed in a comparison between the affection of his subjects and the Gods' regard for Jupiter. The text says that his subjects' affectionate concern for him was no less pleasing than the Gods' response to Jupiter.

l: Augustus Cæsar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cæsar is mentioned in a comparison involving an impious band that sought to extinguish the Roman name in his blood. That attempted violence caused the human race to be astonished by the prospect of universal ruin and made the whole earth shake with horror.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ovid is described as following the prevailing tradition concerning a divine punishment of mankind by a deluge. In the account, Jupiter calls the Gods to a grand council to deliberate about punishing mankind for its wickedness. The explanation compares this tradition with Scripture's account of God deciding to destroy the corrupt earth and its living creatures by a flood. Tradition preserves one just man, whom it identifies as Deucalion, corresponding to Noah in Scripture.

l: Ovid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ovid is said to follow the prevailing tradition of his time in describing a divine decision to punish mankind by a deluge. His account has Jupiter call the Gods together to deliberate about mankind's wickedness.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter calls the Gods to a grand council to deliberate upon the punishment of mankind for its wickedness.

l: Scripture, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Scripture records that God saw mankind's great wickedness and determined to destroy man, beast, creeping thing, and the fowls of the air from the earth.

l: Deucalion's deluge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The deluge is presented as the punishment by which the earth and mankind are to be destroyed because of universal corruption.

l: grand council of the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The grand council of the Gods is convened by Jupiter to deliberate about the punishment of wicked mankind.

l: mankind, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Mankind is described as broadly corrupt and wicked, with the imagination of its thoughts characterized as continually evil. It is marked for destruction in the divine punishment.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The earth is described as suffering from the great wickedness of mankind. Scripture says that God resolves to destroy living creatures from its face.

l: God, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: God sees that mankind's wickedness is great and decides to destroy man and other living creatures from the earth.

l: Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Deucalion is credited by tradition with being at least one just man amid the universal corruption. The explanation says that he possesses the merit attributed to Noah in Scripture.

l: Noah, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Noah is identified as the just man whose merit corresponds to the merit attributed to Deucalion in the tradition described.

l: tradition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Tradition is said to preserve the account of a divine decision to punish the earth by a deluge and to preserve the fact that at least one just man remained amid universal corruption. It attributes this just man's merit to Deucalion, corresponding to Noah in Scripture.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Lycaon, king of Arcadia, tests whether the visiting Jupiter is truly a God by preparing a murderous feast and serving the cooked body of a hostage from the nation of the Molossians. Jupiter destroys Lycaon's house and transforms him into a wolf, who retains traces of his former appearance and continues to desire blood. Jupiter declares that savage Erinnys reigns throughout the earth because men have become wicked. He resolves that all men should soon experience the vengeance they deserve.

l: Lycaon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Lycaon, king of Arcadia, mocks the people's prayers and tests whether Jupiter is a God by planning to kill him in his sleep. He kills a hostage from the nation of the Molossians, cooks the body, and serves it at a feast; Jupiter then destroys his house, and Lycaon becomes a wolf.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter visits Lycaon's palace and gives a sign that a God has come, prompting the people to worship him. In punishment for Lycaon's crimes, Jupiter destroys the house and transforms Lycaon into a wolf; he then declares that all wicked men deserve vengeance.

l: hostage (from the nation of the Molossians), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The hostage from the nation of the Molossians is killed by Lycaon. Lycaon softens part of the hostage's body in boiling water, roasts the rest over a fire, and serves it at the feast.

l: wolf (Lycaon's transformed form), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The wolf is Lycaon's transformed form after Jupiter's punishment. It retains traces of Lycaon's former appearance, including his hoariness, violent features, and bright eyes, while continuing to desire slaughter and blood.

l: savage Erinnys, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Savage Erinnys is said to reign wherever the earth extends. Her rule is associated with the wickedness of men and the vengeance they deserve.

l: mortals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Men are described as if they had conspired to be wicked. Jupiter determines that all men should quickly experience the vengeance they deserve to endure.

l: Lycaon's transformation into a wolf, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Lycaon's transformation occurs as Jupiter's punishment after Lycaon kills and serves the hostage. His garments become hair, his arms become legs, and he becomes a wolf while retaining vestiges of his former form.

l: vengeance, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Vengeance is carried out against Lycaon when Jupiter overturns his house and transforms him into a wolf. Jupiter also declares that all wicked men should soon feel the vengeance they deserve.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The notes discuss Lycaon’s story, including the claim that he served human flesh to Jupiter and was transformed into a wolf. They question whether Ovid’s account contains an anachronism and suggest that Lycaon’s story may derive from the antediluvian story of Cain. Pausanias and Suidas are said to distinguish between two Lycaons, with the second associated with human sacrifice to Jupiter. The explanation compares Lycaon’s punishment with Cain’s sentence to wander the earth.

l: Lycaon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Lycaon is described as the figure who set human flesh before Jupiter and was punished by being transformed into a wolf. The text suggests that his story may preserve elements of the account of Cain, while also reporting that some writers distinguished two Lycaons.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter is the deity before whom Lycaon is said to have set human flesh. In the explanation, Jupiter is also associated with an altar at Lycosura where human victims were sacrificed.

l: Cain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Cain is proposed as a possible original for the story of Lycaon. Both are described as first murderers, and Cain killed Abel while Abel was offering sacrifice; Cain was also personally called to account by the Almighty and sentenced to wander the earth.

l: wolf, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The wolf is presented as the form into which Lycaon was transformed. Its character as a creature shunned by humans and animals is compared with Cain’s punishment as a fugitive and wanderer.

l: human sacrifice, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Human sacrifice is central to the explanation of Lycaon’s story: Lycaon is said to have served human flesh to Jupiter, and the second Lycaon is said to have sacrificed human victims at Lycosura. The tradition is presented as a possible source of the story told by the poet.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter decides that the corruption of mankind requires the destruction of the human race by a universal deluge. He abandons thunderbolts as the means of punishment and sends rain across the earth, while Neptune assists by releasing the rivers and opening the sources of the waters. The flood overwhelms the Earth, blurs the boundary between land and sea, and destroys or carries away people, animals, buildings, crops, and temples. Most living creatures perish, while those spared by the water are overcome by prolonged fasting and lack of food.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter resolves to destroy the corrupt human race by a universal deluge. He chooses rain rather than thunderbolts, sends the South Wind, releases the rains from the whole tract of Heaven, and commands that the rest of the punishment be left to his care.

l: mortals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The human race is condemned by Jupiter because of its universal corruption. It is overwhelmed by the flood, with most people carried away or destroyed and the survivors eventually overcome by hunger.

l: Deucalion's deluge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The universal deluge is the punishment Jupiter uses to destroy mankind. It covers the land, removes the distinction between sea and land, and carries away crops, groves, animals, people, houses, and temples.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Earth is struck by Neptune's trident, which opens the sources of its waters. Its plains, hills, groves, fields, houses, and temples are submerged or swept away.

l: Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The sea expands until it overwhelms the hills and reaches the mountain heights. It has no distinct shores, and its waves carry away people, animals, buildings, and vegetation.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Neptune assists Jupiter with his waves during the deluge. He summons the rivers, orders them to release their full force, and strikes the Earth with his trident to open the sources of its waters.

l: rivers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The rivers gather at Neptune's command, open the mouths of their fountains, and flow unobstructed into the ocean. They break across the plains and carry away crops, groves, flocks, people, houses, temples, and sacred utensils.

l: rain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Rain is released from the whole tract of Heaven as Jupiter's chosen means of punishment. It falls in torrents after the South Wind squeezes the hanging clouds, beating down the standing corn and contributing to the universal flood.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains that Ovid’s account concerns the deluge of Deucalion, one of the five floods mentioned by Pausanias. Although the deluge was generally said to have covered only Thessaly, Ovid adopts the tradition of a universal flood, with waters from the sea joining those from heaven. Deucalion and Pyrrha are presented as counterparts to Noah and his family, and both pairs are said to have been saved for their virtue. The account also compares Parnassus with Mount Ararat and notes that Deucalion’s deluge, like Noah’s flood, was to be the last.

l: Ovid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ovid writes about the deluge of Deucalion and adopts the tradition of a universal flood, although the event was generally said to have affected Thessaly only. He is also said to commit anachronism by mentioning frankincense in an early age when corn or wheaten flour was the customary offering.

l: Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Deucalion is presented as the survivor of a great deluge, together with Pyrrha, because of his virtuous conduct. After being saved, he raised an altar to Jupiter the Liberator, and his story is compared with that of Noah.

l: Noah, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Noah and his family are presented as counterparts to Deucalion and Pyrrha. Noah was saved for his virtuous conduct and offered solemn sacrifices to God after leaving the ark.

l: Thessaly, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Thessaly is identified as the region that the deluge of Deucalion was generally said to have overflowed, although Ovid’s narrative follows the tradition of a universal flood.

l: Parnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Parnassus is described in Ovid’s account as the only mountain whose top remained uncovered by the flood. The explanation suggests that this tradition probably referred to Mount Ararat instead.

l: Mount Ararat, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Mount Ararat is identified as the likely counterpart of Parnassus in the tradition followed by Ovid, because Noah’s ark was said to have rested there.

l: Deucalion's deluge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Deucalion’s deluge is described as one of the two most celebrated floods mentioned by Pausanias. It was generally said to have covered Thessaly, was treated by Ovid as a universal flood, and was to be the last deluge.

l: the flood of Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The flood of Deucalion is the subject of Ovid’s narrative in this unit. Its waters are said to have included both the sea and rain from heaven, and its survivors were Deucalion and Pyrrha.

l: flood of Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Noah’s flood is compared with the flood of Deucalion. Both accounts include virtuous survivors, a solemn offering or altar after deliverance, and a promise or claim that the flood would be the last.

l: tradition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The universal flood tradition is described as a story preserved by all nations and adopted by Ovid in his account of Deucalion. It includes the joining of the sea’s waters with those falling from heaven and is compared with the account of Noah’s flood.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Neptune commands Triton to sound his shell, causing the sea and rivers to retreat within their shores and banks. Deucalion and Pyrrha, the only surviving people, come to rest on Mount Parnassus and worship the gods and Themis. Jupiter clears the clouds and reveals the Earth as the waters subside, while Neptune restores order to the sea. Seeing the empty world, Deucalion tells Pyrrha that they alone remain of the mortal race.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Neptune appeases the angry waves and commands Triton to sound his shell so that the sea may retire within its shores and the rivers within their banks. He lays aside his three-forked trident, assuages the waters, and calls upon Triton to signal their retreat.

l: Triton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Triton stands above the deep with his shoulders covered by native purple shells. At Neptune's command, he blows his resounding trumpet, whose signal is heard by the waters and causes them to stop and retreat.

l: Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Deucalion is the only man saved from the deluge and reaches Parnassus in a little ship with Pyrrha. He is described as the most upright and greatest lover of justice, and he worships the Corycian Nymphs, the mountain deities, and Themis. After the waters recede, he mourns the empty world and tells Pyrrha that they alone remain.

l: Pyrrha, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pyrrha is the only woman saved from the deluge and reaches Parnassus with Deucalion. She is described as more regardful of the deities than any other woman. Deucalion addresses her as his sister and wife and grieves at the thought of their being the only survivors.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter sees that the world has been overwhelmed and that only Deucalion and Pyrrha remain, both guiltless and worshippers of the gods. He disperses the clouds, removes the showers with the North Wind, and exposes the Earth and the heavens to one another.

l: Themis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Themis is prophetic and at that time gives out oracular responses. Deucalion and Pyrrha worship her after reaching Parnassus.

l: Phocis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Phocis separates the Aonian from the Actaean region. It was once fruitful land, but during the deluge it becomes part of the sea and a wide plain of sudden waters.

l: Parnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Parnassus is a lofty mountain with two tops that rises toward the stars and extends its summit beyond the clouds. Deucalion and Pyrrha come to rest there after the sea covers all other places.

l: universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The world is overflowed by liquid waters, leaving only Deucalion and Pyrrha alive from the many thousands who had lived. After Jupiter disperses the clouds and the waters retreat, the world is restored, though it appears empty and silent to Deucalion.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Earth is covered by the waters and later becomes visible as Jupiter clears the clouds and the sea subsides. Its hills emerge, its ground rises, its places increase as the waters decrease, and its woods eventually show their tops while retaining mud on their branches.

l: Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The sea covers all places except where Deucalion and Pyrrha take refuge. Neptune assuages it, and after Triton sounds the retreat, it again has a shore.

l: waters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The waters overflow the world and cover the Earth. At Neptune's command and after Triton's signal, they retreat: the rivers return to their channels, subside, and reveal the hills and woods.

l: Deucalion's deluge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The deluge covers the land and leaves Deucalion and Pyrrha as the only surviving man and woman. It transforms Phocis into part of the sea and a wide plain of waters.

l: the restoration of the world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The restoration of the world begins when Jupiter disperses the clouds and Neptune causes the waters to retreat. The rivers return to their channels, the hills and woods reappear, and the world is again visible, though desolate.

l: the conch shell, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Triton's shell is a hollow-wreathed trumpet that widens from its lowest twist. When Triton blows it at Neptune's command, its sound reaches the shores under both suns and signals the retreat of the waters.

l: mortals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The mortal race is reduced to Deucalion and Pyrrha after the waters destroy the rest of the people. Deucalion wishes that he could replace the lost people by his father's arts and infuse souls into molded earth.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto are described as three brothers who were associated with separate kingdoms and, after being deified, with divisions of the world. Neptune received sovereignty over the sea and was occupied with raising and calming it. The unit depicts Neptune commanding the sea to become orderly, with Triton sounding the retreat on his conch shell. Prometheus and Epimetheus are identified as the fathers of Deucalion and Pyrrha, respectively, and Deucalion invokes the arts of his father Prometheus.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter is described as one of three brothers who may originally have been kings of separate kingdoms. After being deified, he was depicted as retaining sovereignty over his kingdom in the division of the world.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Neptune is described as one of three brothers who was depicted as receiving the empire of the sea. He raises and calms the seas, and in this unit he commands the sea and its waters to return to order.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pluto is described as one of three brothers who may originally have been kings of separate kingdoms. After being deified, he was depicted as retaining sovereignty over his kingdom in the division of the world.

l: Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The sea falls under Neptune’s sovereignty. It is raised or calmed by Neptune, and in this unit it is brought into an orderly state by his commands.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Deucalion and Pyrrha seek Themis's help after the loss of their race and pray at her neglected temple. Themis tells them to cover their heads, loosen their garments, and throw the bones of their great mother behind them. Deucalion interprets the “bones” as stones from the body of the earth, and they cast stones behind them. The stones transform into human forms, renewing the human race.

l: Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Deucalion prays with Pyrrha for guidance on repairing the loss of their race. He interprets Themis's obscure response to mean that they should throw stones, which he and Pyrrha then do.

l: Pyrrha, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pyrrha prays with Deucalion and initially refuses to cast what she thinks are the bones of her mother. After Deucalion explains the response, she joins him in throwing stones, and the female race is renewed through her throwing.

l: Themis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Themis is consulted by Deucalion and Pyrrha at her neglected temple. She is moved by their prayer and gives them the response that leads to the renewal of the human race.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The earth is identified as the great mother whose bones are meant in Themis's response. Its stones are understood to be the bones lying in its body.

l: Themis's response, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Themis's response instructs Deucalion and Pyrrha to depart, cover their heads, loosen their garments, and throw behind them the bones of their great mother. Though initially obscure, it is interpreted as an order to cast stones from the earth.

l: stones as ancestors of humanity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The stones cast behind Deucalion and Pyrrha gradually lose their hardness and stiffness and assume human forms. Those thrown by Deucalion become men, while those thrown by Pyrrha renew the female race.

l: mankind, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The human race, whose loss Deucalion and Pyrrha seek to repair, is renewed through the transformation of the stones. The resulting generation is described as hardy and able to endure fatigue.

l: repopulation of the earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The repopulation of the earth occurs when Deucalion and Pyrrha cast stones behind them as Themis commands. Through the intervention of the Gods above, the stones become men and women.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the flood story of Deucalion and Pyrrha, who fled to Mount Parnassus when Thessaly was inundated. The river Peneus was probably stopped by an earthquake, while extraordinary rainfall caused the flooding. After the waters abated, the children of the survivors were said to be stones, possibly reflecting words meaning both “stone” and “child.” Deucalion later went to Athens, where he built a temple to Jupiter and instituted sacrifices.

l: Parnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Deucalion and some of his subjects fled to Mount Parnassus during the flooding of Thessaly. They remained there until the waters abated.

l: Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Deucalion was king of Thessaly and fled with some of his subjects to Mount Parnassus during the inundation. He later went to Athens, built a temple to Jupiter, and instituted sacrifices in his honor. He was the son of Prometheus and was worshipped as a Divinity after his death.

l: Thessaly, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Thessaly was flooded during the reign of Deucalion after the course of the river Peneus was stopped and an extraordinary quantity of rain fell.

l: Peneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The course of the river Peneus was stopped, probably by an earthquake, before Thessaly was inundated.

l: rainfall and the flooding of Thessaly, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: In the same year that the course of the Peneus was stopped, an immense quantity of rain fell and overflowed all Thessaly. Deucalion and some of his subjects survived by fleeing to Mount Parnassus.

l: stones as ancestors of humanity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The children of those preserved from the inundation were said to be the stones mentioned by the Poet. The explanation connects this fable with words that could mean either “stone” or “child,” and notes that a word meaning “people” could also mean “stone.”

l: Pyrrha, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pyrrha was the wife of Deucalion and the daughter of his uncle, Epimetheus. She was descended from the Titans because her grandfather, Iapetus, was the son of Titan and Terra.

l: Athens, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: After the inundation, Deucalion is said to have gone to Athens. There he built a temple to Jupiter and instituted sacrifices in his honor; some accounts place this under the reign of Cranaus, while Eusebius places it under Cecrops.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Earth, heated by the sun and nourished by moisture, produces animals from the mixture of heat and wetness. Among the creatures it produces is the enormous serpent Python, which terrifies the new race of men. Apollo kills Python with many arrows and establishes the Pythian games to preserve the memory of the deed. The games include contests in boxing, running, and chariot-racing, with crowns of beechen leaves awarded to the winners.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Earth produces animals when moisture and heat are properly mixed and the soil is warmed by the sun. After the deluge, it restores some former shapes and creates new monsters, including Python.

l: Python, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Python is an enormous serpent produced by the Earth, so vast that it occupies a great part of a mountain. It terrifies the new race of men, but Apollo kills it with a thousand arrows.

l: Phœbus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Apollo, the god who bears the bow, kills Python with many arrows, nearly exhausting his quiver as venom oozes from the serpent's wounds. He establishes sacred games called the Pythian games to preserve the fame of this deed.

l: Pythian games, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Pythian games are sacred contests instituted by Apollo in memory of his defeat of Python. Young men compete in boxing, running, and chariot-racing, and the victors receive crowns of beechen leaves.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the serpent Python as either noxious reptiles formed from flood slime and destroyed by the sun’s heat, or a robber near Parnassus defeated by Apollo or an Apollo-associated priest. It connects Python’s destruction with the institution of the Pythian games near Delphi. The games began perhaps as a religious or musical contest honoring the Pythian God and later included athletic and equestrian events. The explanation notes that this event must have occurred much later than the time of Deucalion, when Themis, rather than Apollo, delivered the oracles at Delphi.

l: Pythian games, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Pythian games were celebrated near Delphi and included musical contests, as well as singing, dancing, instrumental music, gymnastic exercises, and equestrian events. They were originally held every eighth year and later every fourth year; their victors first received crowns of beechen leaves and later laurel chaplets with palm branches.

l: Delphi, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Delphi was the place near which the Pythian games were celebrated. Before Apollo’s worship was known there, Themis delivered oracles at Delphi, and before Themis, the Earth delivered them.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Apollo is presented either as the god whose heat destroyed noxious exhalations or as a prince bearing his name, or a priest of his god, who destroyed the serpent Python or a robber near Parnassus. The explanation states that Apollo’s worship was not yet known at Delphi in the time of Deucalion.

l: Python, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The serpent Python is explained philosophically as representing reptiles produced from slime left by the receding flood and then destroyed by the sun’s heat. Historically, it may have represented a robber who troubled people traveling near Parnassus to offer sacrifices.

l: the flood of Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The flood is described as leaving slime as its waters receded. Reptiles were believed to have been produced from this slime and to have disappeared when the sun’s heat dissipated the resulting noxious exhalations.

l: robber near Parnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The robber near Parnassus is proposed as the historical figure represented by the serpent Python. He infested the neighborhood and molested people traveling there to offer sacrifices until a prince named Apollo or a priest of Apollo destroyed him.

l: Pythian games institution, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The institution of the Pythian games is attributed in the explanation to the destruction of the serpent Python or the robber near Parnassus. The games were probably originally a religious ceremony or a musical contest honoring the Pythian God, though later accounts added gymnastic and equestrian competitions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Apollo falls in love with Daphne, the daughter of Peneus, after Cupid wounds him with a golden arrow. Daphne, struck by Cupid’s leaden arrow, rejects love and flees from Apollo, eventually praying to her father and the powers of nature for rescue. Her body is transformed into a laurel tree, which Apollo adopts as his sacred tree and promises to honor in triumphs and before Augustus’s doors.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Apollo, proud of having subdued the Python, mocks Cupid’s use of the bow and claims that archery better suits him. Cupid wounds him with a golden arrow, causing him to love Daphne, whom he pursues and praises. After Daphne becomes a laurel, Apollo declares that the tree will adorn his hair, lyre, and quiver and will receive lasting honors.

l: Daphne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Daphne, the daughter of Peneus, loves the woods, hunting, and perpetual virginity, and rejects all suitors. Wounded by Cupid’s leaden arrow, she flees from Apollo until her strength fails and she asks for divine aid. She is then transformed into a laurel tree, retaining only her former elegance.

l: Peneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Peneus is Daphne’s father, and he repeatedly urges her to accept a husband and give him grandchildren. Daphne appeals to him for aid when Apollo is about to overtake her.

l: Cupid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cupid assigns Daphne to Apollo in vengeance after Apollo mocks him and his weapons. He uses two arrows: a golden arrow that excites desire and a leaden arrow that repels it, striking Apollo and Daphne respectively.

l: laurel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The laurel is the form Daphne takes after her prayer for rescue. Apollo adopts it as his tree and says it will adorn his hair, lyre, and quiver, accompany triumphal processions, and stand as a guardian before Augustus’s doors.

l: Apollo and Daphne's pursuit, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Apollo pursues Daphne because Cupid’s golden arrow has made him love her, while Cupid’s leaden arrow makes her flee from the very idea of love. Apollo follows her through the woods, comparing their chase to animals pursuing or escaping one another, until she reaches the waters of Peneus.

l: Daphne's transformation into a laurel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: When Daphne prays for aid, a heavy torpor seizes her limbs and her body changes into a laurel. Bark covers her breasts, her hair becomes leaves, her arms become branches, and her feet take root, while her former elegance remains.

l: Love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Love is presented as the force that makes Apollo pursue Daphne and as the cause of his wound. Apollo says that love cannot be cured by herbs, even though he is the discoverer of healing and the properties of simples.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: This unit explains notes and interpretations concerning Apollo’s pursuit of Daphne and her transformation into a laurel. Apollo is identified with the Delian God, a youthful deity associated with the lyre, healing herbs, prophecy, the sun, and victory. Daphne flees Apollo to the river Peneus, while later explanations connect her name or nearby laurels with the transformation story. Alternative accounts identify Daphne with Manto or describe her as the victim of an incident involving Leucippus and Apollo.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Apollo is called the Delian God because he was believed to have been born on Delos. He is portrayed as a perpetually youthful deity associated with the sun, the lyre, healing herbs, prophecy, and victory; laurel crowns are connected with his musicians and triumphs.

l: Daphne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Daphne is the maiden pursued by Apollo toward the river Peneus. The explanation suggests that her name, which means laurel in Greek, may have helped give rise to the story of her transformation; Diodorus Siculus identifies her with Manto, the daughter of Tiresias.

l: Peneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Peneus is identified as a river of Thessaly. Daphne is said to have fled toward its bank, where one explanation holds that she was accidentally precipitated into the river and perished in Apollo’s sight.

l: laurel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Laurel is associated with Daphne’s transformation and with Apollo’s lyre, triumphs, and civic honors. The explanation proposes that laurels growing near the place where Daphne perished, or the Greek meaning of her name, may have inspired the transformation story.

l: Apollo and Daphne's pursuit, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Apollo pursues Daphne as she flees, and the chase is compared with a greyhound pursuing a hare. The comparison emphasizes Apollo’s eagerness and Daphne’s anxiety as she tries to escape.

l: Daphne's transformation into a laurel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The explanation treats Daphne’s transformation as possibly arising from laurels growing near the place where she died or from the meaning of her name, Daphne, which is Greek for laurel. It also records alternative accounts in which Daphne is Manto or in which Apollo exposes Leucippus’s disguise, after which Daphne and her companions kill him.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter pursues Io, the daughter of Inachus, as she returns from her father's stream. He invites her into the groves of Tempe, claiming he will protect her, but she flees from him. Jupiter covers the earth with darkness, stops her flight, and ravishes her. Inachus, unaware of what has happened, mourns Io and fears that she is dead.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter sees Io returning from her father's stream and pursues her. He invites her into the groves, promises protection, covers the earth with darkness, stops her flight, and ravishes her.

l: Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Io is the daughter of Inachus. She flees from Jupiter after he invites her into the groves, but he overtakes her when darkness covers the earth and ravishes her.

l: Inachus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Inachus is absent from the gathering of the rivers and remains hidden in his deepest cavern. He increases his waters with tears and mourns Io, fearing that she is dead or among the shades below.

l: Tempe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Tempe is a grove of Hæmonia enclosed by a wood on every side and situated among craggy rocks. The river Peneus flows through it, and it is the home and retreat of that river and of the Nymphs inhabiting its waters.

l: Peneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Peneus flows from the bottom of Pindus through Tempe with foaming waves. Its fall gathers clouds and spray, and its noise reaches places far away.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The earth is covered far and wide with darkness by Jupiter while he pursues Io.

l: darkness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Darkness is spread over the earth by Jupiter. It enables him to arrest Io's flight.

l: Jupiter's pursuit of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter's pursuit begins when he sees Io returning from Inachus's stream. He follows her past the pastures of Lerna and the Lircæan plains, then uses darkness to stop her.

l: Jupiter's ravishment of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter's ravishment of Io occurs after he has covered the earth with darkness and arrested her flight. The text presents it as the forcing of Io's modesty.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains that the story of Io probably originated in Egypt and was incorporated into Greek mythology through the spread of Isis worship to Greece. It identifies Io with Isis and says that Greek authors described Io as the daughter of Inachus, whom Jupiter carried away and by whom he had Epaphus. Juno, jealous of Jupiter's intrigue, placed Io under the watch of Argus, but Jupiter killed Argus and had Io taken aboard a vessel shaped like a cow. The notes also describe Thessalian rivers and places mentioned in the surrounding passage, including Tempe, Pindus, Spercheus, Enipeus, Apidanus, Amphrysus, Æas, Inachus, and Lerna.

l: Inachus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Inachus is described as the first king of Argos and the father of Io according to Greek authors. He is also said to have gone to settle in Greece, where the worship of Isis was received.

l: Egypt, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Egypt is presented as the probable source of the story of Io. Isis was one of its chief divinities, and Epaphus went there to reign after being born to Io and Jupiter.

l: Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Greece received the worship of Isis when Inachus went there to settle. In the course of time, Isis was identified there with Io, and a related fable was developed.

l: Isis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Isis was one of the chief divinities of Egypt. Her worship passed into foreign countries, including Greece, where she was eventually identified with Io.

l: Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Io is presented as the Greek form of the Egyptian Isis and, according to Greek authors, as the daughter of Inachus. Jupiter carried her away, fathered Epaphus by her, and she later accompanied Epaphus to Egypt.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter carried Io away and had Epaphus by her. After Juno placed Io under Argus's care, Jupiter killed Argus and placed Io aboard a vessel with a cow's figure at its head.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Juno discovered Jupiter's intrigue and, driven by jealousy, placed Io under the care of Argus.

l: Argus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Argus was Io's uncle and was described as a man of great vigilance. Juno entrusted Io to him, but Jupiter later killed him.
